title: Why Leaders Must Get Good at Arguing
author: Deasy, Derek et al.
summary: Derek Deasy and Enoch Li argue that leaders should stop treating workplace conflict as something to suppress and instead use it deliberately to build team resilience, defined as the capacity to maximize learning from setbacks. Their three-step method starts with recognizing that a leader's own stress is compounded by the team's collective, often unconscious anxiety about survival and belonging, then moves to examining the habitual assumptions (like reading a question as a personal attack) that turn ordinary disagreement into stalemate, and finally requires leaders to have the courage to name the unspoken 'elephant in the room' directly with the whole team rather than just the immediate parties to a dispute. The piece frames psychologically difficult feelings — shame, jealousy, loneliness — as inevitable and useful data about group dynamics rather than problems to be moralized away. It closes by tying diversity of perspective explicitly to disagreement, arguing that eliminating friction would also eliminate the creativity that disagreement makes possible.
points: Reframes conflict as a resilience-building opportunity rather than a failure state to be avoided.
A leader's own anxiety is compounded by absorbing the team's collective, often unconscious fears about survival and belonging.
Diverting blame during failure is often really about protecting a leader's own sense of competence, not a fair read of what happened.
The productive move is pushing conversation past 'what happened' into 'how did we feel' and 'what did those feelings make us do to each other.'
Argues eliminating disagreement would also eliminate the diversity, creativity, and innovation that disagreement makes possible.
quotes: From disagreements over the right strategy to adopt to heated recriminations following a project failure, conflicts are a regular part of business life. But most leaders and teams view conflict as a negative that should be avoided at all costs.

Developing a sustainable approach to building resilience in the face of change and conflict first requires leaders to understand that workplace dynamics are deeply interconnected. How leaders process stress and tension is impacted by the specific contexts they're operating in: the people with whom they work, and the different ways those individuals process their own stress.

A group's anxiety typically comes from fears of survival and doubts over whether people truly care for one another. If these anxieties are suppressed, this can lead to interactions that seem polite enough on the surface but are emotionally distant or inauthentic.

Failure can make us feel incompetent and ashamed, so when something goes wrong, energy is often spent diverting the blame. A leader might criticise others for resisting their ideas, when the truth is the leader actually feels insecure about their own abilities.
The key is to get beyond the "what happened" part of the conversation to tackle the "how did we feel" dimension and explore "what these feelings made us do to each other".
Discontent, arguments and disagreements are all part of daily work and leadership. If everyone saw things the same way, we would lose our diversity, creativity and innovation.
